newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Western Australia calls for decision on Gorgon gas.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Western Australia calls for decision on Gorgon gas.

text.p: Western Australia's Minister for Resources Development, Colin Barnett, on Thursday called for the principal players involved in the liquefied natural gas (LNG) industry to decide on the future development of the industry.

Barnett told a Perth business luncheon the LNG market internationally was growing "very very strongly" and Western Australia was well placed to take advantage of the resulting opportunities because of its large LNG reserves.

However, he said he had a "growing sense of frustration and impatience" at the "international corporate by-play" going on between the partners involved in the North West Shelf and the Gorgon projects, over how local production will be expanded.

Barnett said that while the partners "give contradictory conflicting statements to the market" about whether a joint venture is possible, there was a danger not only of Australia losing market opportunities but also of damage to Western Australia's international reputation.

"I don't want to interfere and I am not about to interfere, in those projects, but I think the time has arrived for the Government to take a more proactive stand in bringing those projects to a decision making stage," Barnett said.
"We really don't care which way they go but I think it is time a decision was made," he said.
The North West Shelf has a total production capacity of about 7.5 million tonnes per annum (mtpa) and the joint venture participants are currently assessing the viability of almost doubling that.
The Gorgon LNG project, which has the capacity to produce about 6 mtpa, is currently the subject of feasibility studies.

Barnett acknowledged there were two possible scenarios for the two projects - they could each go it alone or set up a joint venture that would allow the Gorgon project to tap the North West Shelf's existing infrastructure while making the Gorgon reserves available to satisfy the Western Australian market.

"I have consistently maintained the position that the decision is one for the parties involved," he said. "However the decision has taken some time to be made and certainly I have a growing sense of frustration and a growing sense of impatience
because there are some issues that go beyond the private commercial interests of the two joint ventures," Barnett said.

"While there is an international corporate by-play as to which project will go ahead, and while individual joint venture partners give contradictory, conflicting statements to the market, one person saying we will do a joint project and another person saying 'no way', there is a danger, indeed the prospect, that Australia will lose market opportunities," he said. "That becomes something of interest to the Australian government and certainly to the Western Australian Government."
